slides.body: Four questions a CTO can ask, calmly, after a week in which someone rebased.
"Asha pushed a commit to the feature branch on Tuesday. On Wednesday it was gone from GitHub, and after her next pull it was gone from her laptop as well. Nobody deleted anything. Where is it?"
"The pull request had three commits before the review and three commits after it, with the same titles. The reviewer approved the first version. What exactly is different in the second one?"
"Why does the history of the ingest branch contain every commit twice?"
"A developer says the rebase finished without an error and one of his commits is not in the branch any more. Is that possible?"
The fourth answer is "yes". Hold on to that one.
Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery.

items: Saying "rebase moved my commits" and then looking for the old IDs on the branch. Root cause: a commit object is never modified; rebase wrote new objects and moved one ref.
Expecting the same ID because the diff is identical. Root cause: the ID hashes the commit object, whose parent, committer and usually tree changed; the patch ID is what stayed the same.
Believing the originals are deleted. Root cause: nothing was removed from the object database; ORIG_HEAD and the branch's reflog still name the old tip.
Thinking the branch "remembers" where it started. Root cause: Git has no notion of a parent branch; the commits to replay are computed by reachability from the graph.

Rebasing and assuming everything that recorded an old ID still points at your work. Root cause: review comments, CI statuses, deployment records and tags refer to commit IDs, and those commits are no longer on the branch.

beats.text: In one sentence: git rebase <upstream> 🟡 CAUTION takes the commits that your branch has and <upstream> doesn't have, creates a copy of each one on top of <upstream>, in order, and then points your branch at the last copy.
beats.tele: In one sentence: `git rebase <upstream>` 🟡 CAUTION takes the commits that your branch has and `<upstream>` doesn't have, creates a copy of each one on top of `<upstream>`, in order, and then points your branch at the last copy.

beats.text: Why would you want that? There are two everyday uses. One is bringing a feature branch up to date before review, so that the reviewer and CI, the automated checks, see your change on top of today's main. The other is tidying your own commits before anyone else reads them.
beats.tele: Why would you want that? There are two everyday uses. One is bringing a feature branch up to date before review, so that the reviewer and CI, the automated checks, see your change on top of today's `main`. The other is tidying your own commits before anyone else reads them.

beats.text: Precisely. The manual describes git rebase <upstream> as four steps.
beats.tele: Precisely. The manual describes `git rebase <upstream>` as four steps.

beats.text: One. Make the list of commits to replay: everything reachable from the current branch and not from <upstream>, the same set that git log <upstream>..HEAD prints, minus commits whose change is already in <upstream>, and minus merge commits. Both exceptions get their own videos. On screen, the list is the three commits of feat/rerank.
beats.tele: One. Make the list of commits to replay: everything reachable from the current branch and not from `<upstream>`, the same set that `git log <upstream>..HEAD` prints, minus commits whose change is already in `<upstream>`, and minus merge commits. Both exceptions get their own videos. On screen, the list is the three commits of `feat/rerank`.

beats.text: Two. Detach HEAD at <upstream>. Detached means that HEAD names a commit directly, here the tip of main, and not a branch.
beats.tele: Two. Detach HEAD at `<upstream>`. Detached means that HEAD names a commit directly, here the tip of `main`, and not a branch.

beats.text: Three. Replay the commits one by one, oldest first. Each replay is a cherry-pick: one commit's change, applied on top of HEAD as a new commit. Inside, it's a three-way merge whose base is the parent of the original commit, whose "ours" side is HEAD, and whose "theirs" side is the original commit. The result is committed with the original author, author date and message, and with you, now, as committer.
beats.tele: Three. Replay the commits one by one, oldest first. Each replay is a cherry-pick: one commit's change, applied on top of HEAD as a new commit. Inside, it's a three-way merge whose base is the parent of the original commit, whose "ours" side is HEAD, and whose "theirs" side is the original commit. The result is committed with the original author, author date and message, and with you, now, as committer.

beats.text: Four. Move the branch ref to the last new commit, and attach HEAD to the branch again.
beats.tele: Four. Move the branch ref to the last new commit, and attach HEAD to the branch again.

beats.text: Two words in that description deserve attention. "Reachable": Git has no notion of a parent branch, so the set of commits is computed from the graph, not from where you believe the branch started. And "copy": a commit object is never modified. The copies are new objects with new commit IDs.
beats.tele: Two words in that description deserve attention. "Reachable": Git has no notion of a parent branch, so the set of commits is computed from the graph, not from where you believe the branch started. And "copy": a commit object is never modified. The copies are new objects with new commit IDs.

beats.text: Inside .git: new commit objects, and new tree objects wherever the combined content differs from anything stored before. Blobs, the stored file contents, are reused when file content is unchanged. One branch ref is rewritten, once, at the end. HEAD is detached while the rebase runs. ORIG_HEAD records the old tip. The reflogs of HEAD and of the branch, Git's local lists of where each has been, record every step.
beats.tele: Inside `.git`: new commit objects, and new tree objects wherever the combined content differs from anything stored before. Blobs, the stored file contents, are reused when file content is unchanged. One branch ref is rewritten, once, at the end. HEAD is detached while the rebase runs. `ORIG_HEAD` records the old tip. The reflogs of HEAD and of the branch, Git's local lists of where each has been, record every step.

beats.text: Now the ID. In one sentence: a commit ID is a hash of the commit object, the commit object names its parent and its tree, and a replayed commit has a different parent and usually a different tree, so it can't have the same ID.
beats.tele: Now the ID. In one sentence: a commit ID is a hash of the commit object, the commit object names its parent and its tree, and a replayed commit has a different parent and usually a different tree, so it can't have the same ID.

says: A new parent means a new ID, for this commit and for every commit after it

beats.text: And because each commit names its parent by ID, a new ID for one commit forces a new ID for every commit after it. IDs change from the first rewritten commit onward, never before it.
beats.tele: And because each commit names its parent by ID, a new ID for one commit forces a new ID for every commit after it. IDs change from the first rewritten commit onward, never before it.

beats.text: When not to rebase? The textbook calls it the most important judgment in the chapter. Both everyday uses are safe on a branch that only you use, and both become a team incident on a branch that others have based work on.
beats.tele: When not to rebase? The textbook calls it the most important judgment in the chapter. Both everyday uses are safe on a branch that only you use, and both become a team incident on a branch that others have based work on.

beats.text: A picture helps. The textbook's analogy: you wrote three amendments to version 4 of a contract. Meanwhile the other party issued version 6. Rebasing is redoing your three amendments, one after the other, against version 6, so that the file reads as if you had started from version 6.
beats.tele: A picture helps. The textbook's analogy: you wrote three amendments to version 4 of a contract. Meanwhile the other party issued version 6. Rebasing is redoing your three amendments, one after the other, against version 6, so that the file reads as if you had started from version 6.

beats.text: It breaks in two places, and both are the lesson. First, the three amendments you wrote against version 4 aren't shredded. They stay in the drawer, the object database, reachable through the reflog. Second, nobody retypes anything. Each amendment is carried over by a three-way merge that Git computes, and that merge can stop and ask you to decide.

beats.text: B, the parent, and it's not alone. Three of the five inputs to the hash changed: tree, parent, committer. A copy would get a new ID even with the same parent and tree, because the committer date moves. That's why Git doesn't copy commits that would come out identical. It fast-forwards over them unless you pass --no-ff.

beats.text: Step 3: what did not change. A patch ID is a hash of a commit's diff with line numbers ignored.

beats.text: Same patch ID in the first column, different commit IDs in the second. Git uses this equivalence to recognise "the same change under another ID". You'll meet it again when a rebase drops a commit on purpose. And that's how the CTO's fourth question can be a yes: step one leaves out a commit whose change is already in the upstream, and no error is printed.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Saying "rebase moved my commits" and then looking for the old IDs on the branch. Root cause: a commit object is never modified; rebase wrote new objects and moved one ref.
beats.tele: Saying "rebase moved my commits" and then looking for the old IDs on the branch. Root cause: a commit object is never modified; rebase wrote new objects and moved one ref.

beats.text: Expecting the same ID because the diff is identical. Root cause: the ID hashes the commit object, whose parent, committer and usually tree changed; the patch ID is what stayed the same.
beats.tele: Expecting the same ID because the diff is identical. Root cause: the ID hashes the commit object, whose parent, committer and usually tree changed; the patch ID is what stayed the same.

beats.text: Believing the originals are deleted. Root cause: nothing was removed from the object database; ORIG_HEAD and the branch's reflog still name the old tip.
beats.tele: Believing the originals are deleted. Root cause: nothing was removed from the object database; `ORIG_HEAD` and the branch's reflog still name the old tip.

beats.text: Thinking the branch "remembers" where it started. Root cause: Git has no notion of a parent branch; the commits to replay are computed by reachability from the graph.
beats.tele: Thinking the branch "remembers" where it started. Root cause: Git has no notion of a parent branch; the commits to replay are computed by reachability from the graph.

beats.text: Rebasing and assuming everything that recorded an old ID still points at your work. Root cause: review comments, CI statuses, deployment records and tags refer to commit IDs, and those commits are no longer on the branch.

beats.text: Answer out loud first. A strong answer starts from what a commit ID is computed from, and goes through the fields one by one, saying for each whether it changes and why. It explains why the change propagates to every later commit and never to an earlier one. It names the thing that does stay equal between an original and its copy, and what Git uses it for. If you can add what follows for anything that has stored the old IDs, you have connected the mechanism to practice.
